prime.problem: A tokenizer trained on English has no single symbol for a run of spaces, so Python's indentation costs several tokens on every line. That wastes context and training compute on characters that carry little information.
prime.fits: A preprocessing change inside Codex's training. It's the first card about how the model is built rather than how it's graded, and it builds on the idea that a model sees tokens, not characters.
prime.goal: Compute the token saving on a snippet, convert a percentage saving into context capacity, and say why this is an efficiency change rather than a capability claim.

attend: Why is whitespace the single biggest source of waste when a prose tokenizer reads Python?
Why add tokens to GPT-3's vocabulary rather than train a fresh code tokenizer?
Why can't you just strip indentation before tokenizing Python?
The worked snippet saves 20.7% but the paper reports ~30%. What property of real code explains the gap?

must: Prose tokenizer has no symbol for long space runs → each indented line costs several tokens of whitespace → add one token per run length → indentation becomes about one token per line → ~30% fewer tokens on Python
Fewer tokens for the same code → more code per 2048-token context (≈2,926 old-encoding tokens' worth) and cheaper training per line → an efficiency gain, with no ablation showing a pass@k gain
Keep GPT-3's vocabulary and add to it → English docstrings still tokenize as before → Codex can reuse text representations, which a code-only BPE would throw away
In Python indentation is syntax → it can't be dropped or normalised → it must be encoded, so making it cheap is the right lever; the gain is smaller for brace languages
elevated: Saving scales with nesting depth and blank/alignment whitespace → deeper real code saves more than a shallow 10-line function → quote savings per corpus, not per snippet
reference: the exact per-line token costs in the worked example (illustrative)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3 sentences what the tokenizer change is, what it buys, and what it doesn't claim. Then redo the context arithmetic: how many old-encoding tokens fit in 2048 new ones at a 30% saving?
checklist: GPT-3 text tokenizer plus one token per whitespace-run length
2048 / 0.70 ≈ 2,926 old tokens' worth of code per window
efficiency, not a measured quality gain

retrieve.q: Explain why a prose-trained tokenizer is especially wasteful on Python compared with English text.
answer: prose rarely has long space runs, so BPE never merged them
Python indents nearly every line, often by 4 or 8 spaces
each run gets split into several tokens

retrieve.q: Walk through the worked snippet's arithmetic: where do 58 and 46 come from, and what's the reduction?
Someone proposes training a brand-new BPE on code instead. What would Codex gain and lose?
answer: gain: possibly even shorter code sequences
Codex is prompted with English docstrings, so that loss matters

compare.q: Adding whitespace-run tokens is a specific case of growing a vocabulary. What does each extra token cost the model, and why is this particular addition cheap for what it saves?
answer: each new token adds an embedding row and an output logit
a handful of whitespace tokens is tiny next to the vocabulary
they appear on almost every line of code, so the saving is large

compare.q: Tokenization causes many LLM oddities. Which oddity does this change remove for code, and which kinds of tokenization weirdness does it leave untouched?
answer: removes: indentation eating a large share of the context
leaves: odd splits of identifiers and numbers

predict.q: Codex is later evaluated on a language with braces and little indentation. Would you expect the tokenizer's saving there to be bigger, similar, or smaller than 30%? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Smaller. The saving comes from whitespace runs; brace languages still indent, but indentation isn't required and code is often less deeply nested, so there's less whitespace to compress. The paper only trains and evaluates on Python, so it gives no number.

apply.task: A 12-line function has 50 content tokens, 8 lines indented by 4 spaces and 4 lines by 8 spaces. The text tokenizer spends 2 tokens per 4-space run and 3 per 8-space run; the new tokenizer spends 1 token for either. Compute both totals and the percentage reduction.
apply.done: You get 78 tokens vs 62 tokens, a 20.5% reduction, and you can say why it's below the paper's ~30%.
